Day 1 & 2 · 8 & 9 Oct · Quiz 01

Continuous functions

  • Plug in carefully. "·" means multiply, so look for a zero factor first: ln⁡1=0\ln 1=0ln1=0, sin⁡0=0\sin 0=0sin0=0, cos⁡π2=0,\cos\frac{\pi}{2}=0,cos2π​=0, while e0=1e^0=1e0=1.
  • Inverse trig ranges: arcsin⁡\arcsinarcsin lands in [−π2,π2],[-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}],[−2π​,2π​], arccos⁡\arccosarccos in [0,π][0,\pi][0,π], arctan⁡\arctanarctan in (−π2,π2).(-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}).(−2π​,2π​).
  • Limits: plug in first. A 00\frac{0}{0}00​ result means simplify (factor and cancel, or use the conjugate), then plug in. The limit exists only when the left and right limits agree.
  • Limit laws: if f→Lf\to Lf→L and g→Mg\to Mg→M (numbers), then f±g→L±M,fg→LMfg→LM(M≠0)\begin{gathered}f\pm g\to L\pm M,\qquad fg\to LM\\[4pt]\frac{f}{g}\to\frac{L}{M}\quad(M\ne0)\end{gathered}f±g→L±M,fg→LMgf​→ML​(M=0)​
  • Special limits: lim⁡x→0sin⁡xx=1lim⁡x→01−cos⁡xx=0lim⁡x→0ex−1x=1\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin x}{x}&=1\\[4pt]\lim_{x\to0}\frac{1-\cos x}{x}&=0\\[4pt]\lim_{x\to0}\frac{e^x-1}{x}&=1\end{aligned}x→0lim​xsinx​x→0lim​x1−cosx​x→0lim​xex−1​​=1=0=1​
  • Continuity at aaa: f(a)f(a)f(a) is defined, lim⁡x→af(x)\lim_{x\to a}f(x)limx→a​f(x) exists, and the two are equal. A break is removable (a hole), a jump, or infinite.

Watch out

  • Reading "·" as "+" is an easy slip. Rewrite products with × before you plug in.
  • 00\frac{0}{0}00​ is never the answer. It tells you to simplify first.

Day 3 & 4 · 12 & 13 Oct · Quiz 02

Derivatives of functions and chain rule

  • Definition: f′(x)=lim⁡h→0f(x+h)−f(x)hf'(x)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}f′(x)=h→0lim​hf(x+h)−f(x)​ Tangent line at x0x_0x0​: y=f(x0)+f′(x0)(x−x0)y=f(x_0)+f'(x_0)(x-x_0)y=f(x0​)+f′(x0​)(x−x0​)
  • Rules: (xn)′=nxn−1(fg)′=f′g+fg′(fg)′=f′g−fg′g2\begin{aligned}(x^n)'&=nx^{n-1}\\[2pt](fg)'&=f'g+fg'\\[2pt]\left(\frac{f}{g}\right)'&=\frac{f'g-fg'}{g^2}\end{aligned}(xn)′(fg)′(gf​)′​=nxn−1=f′g+fg′=g2f′g−fg′​​
  • Basic derivatives: (sin⁡x)′=cos⁡x(cos⁡x)′=−sin⁡x(tan⁡x)′=sec⁡2x(ex)′=ex(ax)′=axln⁡a(ln⁡x)′=1x\begin{aligned}(\sin x)'&=\cos x&\quad(\cos x)'&=-\sin x\\[2pt](\tan x)'&=\sec^2x&\quad(e^x)'&=e^x\\[2pt](a^x)'&=a^x\ln a&\quad(\ln x)'&=\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}(sinx)′(tanx)′(ax)′​=cosx=sec2x=axlna​(cosx)′(ex)′(lnx)′​=−sinx=ex=x1​​
  • Chain rule: (f(g(x)))′=f′(g(x))⋅g′(x)\big(f(g(x))\big)'=f'(g(x))\cdot g'(x)(f(g(x)))′=f′(g(x))⋅g′(x) You only need the base formulas: each "u-version" is the base formula times u′u'u′. Example: (ln⁡(cos⁡x))′=−sin⁡xcos⁡x=−tan⁡x\big(\ln(\cos x)\big)'=\frac{-\sin x}{\cos x}=-\tan x(ln(cosx))′=cosx−sinx​=−tanx
  • Higher-order derivatives: f′′=(f′)′f''=(f')'f′′=(f′)′ and f′′′=(f′′)′f'''=(f'')'f′′′=(f′′)′.

Watch out

  • The product rule always has two terms: (x2⋅x3)′=2x⋅x3+x2⋅3x2=5x4.(x^2\cdot x^3)'=2x\cdot x^3+x^2\cdot 3x^2=5x^4.(x2⋅x3)′=2x⋅x3+x2⋅3x2=5x4.
  • In the tangent formula the slope is f′(x0)f'(x_0)f′(x0​). Don't use x0x_0x0​ itself as the slope.
  • Carry the minus from (cos⁡x)′=−sin⁡x(\cos x)'=-\sin x(cosx)′=−sinx all the way to the end.
  • (2x)′=2xln⁡2(2^x)'=2^x\ln 2(2x)′=2xln2, not x⋅2x−1x\cdot 2^{x-1}x⋅2x−1.

Day 5 & 6 · 15 & 16 Oct · Quiz 03

Implicit differentiation and parametric curve

  • Implicit differentiation: differentiate both sides with respect to xxx and attach y′y'y′ to every yyy-term: (y3)′=3y2y′(y^3)'=3y^2y'(y3)′=3y2y′, (sin⁡y)′=cos⁡y⋅y′,(\sin y)'=\cos y\cdot y',(siny)′=cosy⋅y′, (xy)′=y+xy′(xy)'=y+xy'(xy)′=y+xy′. Then collect the y′y'y′ terms and factor.
  • Tangent lines: put both x0x_0x0​ and y0y_0y0​ into y′y'y′, then use y−y0=m(x−x0)y-y_0=m(x-x_0)y−y0​=m(x−x0​). On a circle x2+y2=r2x^2+y^2=r^2x2+y2=r2, y′=−xyy'=-\dfrac{x}{y}y′=−yx​ and the tangent is perpendicular to the radius.
  • Vertical tangent: if y′=NDy'=\dfrac{N}{D}y′=DN​ has D=0D=0D=0 but N≠0N\ne0N=0 at a point, dydx\frac{dy}{dx}dxdy​ doesn't exist and the tangent is vertical. A double root when you plug in xxx is the warning sign.
  • Inverse functions: if f(a)=bf(a)=bf(a)=b, then (f−1)′(b)=1f′(a)(f^{-1})'(b)=\frac{1}{f'(a)}(f−1)′(b)=f′(a)1​ Solve f(a)=bf(a)=bf(a)=b first.
  • Inverse trig: (arcsin⁡x)′=11−x2(arccos⁡x)′=−11−x2(arctan⁡x)′=11+x2\begin{aligned}(\arcsin x)'&=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\\[4pt](\arccos x)'&=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\\[4pt](\arctan x)'&=\frac{1}{1+x^2}\end{aligned}(arcsinx)′(arccosx)′(arctanx)′​=1−x2​1​=−1−x2​1​=1+x21​​
  • Reciprocal trig: (cot⁡x)′=−csc⁡2x,(\cot x)'=-\csc^2x,(cotx)′=−csc2x, (sec⁡x)′=sec⁡xtan⁡x,(\sec x)'=\sec x\tan x,(secx)′=secxtanx, (csc⁡x)′=−csc⁡xcot⁡x.(\csc x)'=-\csc x\cot x.(cscx)′=−cscxcotx.
  • Parametric curves: slope and second derivative: dydx=dy/dtdx/dtd2ydx2=ddt ⁣(dydx)dx/dt\begin{gathered}\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}\\[6pt]\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\frac{\frac{d}{dt}\!\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)}{dx/dt}\end{gathered}dxdy​=dx/dtdy/dt​dx2d2y​=dx/dtdtd​(dxdy​)​​

Watch out

  • Every yyy-term gets a y′y'y′: sin⁡y=x\sin y=xsiny=x gives cos⁡y⋅y′=1\cos y\cdot y'=1cosy⋅y′=1, not cos⁡y=0\cos y=0cosy=0. And dxdx=1\frac{dx}{dx}=1dxdx​=1.
  • Signs at negative points: on x2+y2=10x^2+y^2=10x2+y2=10 at (1,−3)(1,-3)(1,−3), y′=−1−3=+13.y'=-\dfrac{1}{-3}=+\dfrac{1}{3}.y′=−−31​=+31​.
  • In the inverse formula use f′(a)f'(a)f′(a), not f′(b)f'(b)f′(b).
  • The second derivative is not a ratio of second derivatives: d2ydx2≠d2y/dt2d2x/dt2\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\ne\frac{d^2y/dt^2}{d^2x/dt^2}dx2d2y​=d2x/dt2d2y/dt2​

Day 7 & 8 · 19 & 20 Oct · Quiz 04

Maximum and minimum problem

  • Critical points: numbers ccc in the domain where f′(c)=0f'(c)=0f′(c)=0 or f′(c)f'(c)f′(c) doesn't exist.
  • First derivative test: f′f'f′ goes +→−+\to-+→−: relative max. −→+-\to+−→+: relative min. No sign change: neither.
  • Second derivative test (when f′(c)=0f'(c)=0f′(c)=0): f′′(c)<0f''(c)<0f′′(c)<0 means concave down, a relative max. f′′(c)>0f''(c)>0f′′(c)>0 means concave up, a relative min. f′′(c)=0f''(c)=0f′′(c)=0 gives no conclusion.
  • Closed interval method: evaluate fff at the critical points inside [a,b][a,b][a,b] and at both endpoints. The largest value is the absolute max, the smallest the absolute min.
  • Inflection points: where f′′f''f′′ changes sign. Report the point (c,f(c))(c,f(c))(c,f(c)).
  • Logs: ln⁡\lnln is increasing, so compare the insides. On Quiz 04, log⁡\loglog means ln⁡\lnln.

Watch out

  • x2=1x^2=1x2=1 has two roots, x=±1x=\pm1x=±1.
  • ∣x2−2x∣|x^2-2x|∣x2−2x∣ is never negative. Plug into the original absolute value, not into one piece of it.
  • Critical points come from f′=0f'=0f′=0, not f=0f=0f=0.
  • The yyy-coordinate is always f(c)f(c)f(c), never f′(c)f'(c)f′(c) or f′′(c)f''(c)f′′(c).
  • f′′(c)=0f''(c)=0f′′(c)=0 alone doesn't make an inflection point: x4x^4x4 has none at 000.

Day 9 · 22 Oct

Infinite series

  • Sequence limits: divide every term by the highest power of nnn, or by the biggest base. rn→0r^n\to0rn→0 when ∣r∣<1|r|<1∣r∣<1.
  • Partial sums: sN=∑n=0Nan,s_N=\sum_{n=0}^{N}a_n,sN​=∑n=0N​an​, and the infinite series is lim⁡N→∞sN.\lim_{N\to\infty}s_N.limN→∞​sN​.
  • Geometric: the partial sum, and the infinite sum when ∣r∣<1|r|<1∣r∣<1: ∑n=0Nrn=1−rN+11−r∑n=0∞rn=11−r\begin{aligned}\sum_{n=0}^{N}r^n&=\frac{1-r^{N+1}}{1-r}\\[4pt]\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}r^n&=\frac{1}{1-r}\end{aligned}n=0∑N​rnn=0∑∞​rn​=1−r1−rN+1​=1−r1​​ When ∣r∣≥1|r|\ge1∣r∣≥1 it diverges.
  • Tests: if an↛0a_n\not\to0an​→0, the series diverges. Ratio test: r=lim⁡n→∞∣an+1an∣r=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right|r=n→∞lim​​an​an+1​​​ r<1r<1r<1 converges, r>1r>1r>1 diverges, r=1r=1r=1 says nothing.
  • Typical series: ∑1np\sum\dfrac{1}{n^p}∑np1​ converges only when p>1p>1p>1, so the harmonic series ∑1n\sum\dfrac{1}{n}∑n1​ diverges. Telescoping: ∑n=1∞1n(n+1)=1\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n(n+1)}=1n=1∑∞​n(n+1)1​=1
  • Power series: ∑cnxn\sum c_nx^n∑cn​xn converges for ∣x∣<R|x|<R∣x∣<R. Find the radius RRR with the ratio test, then check x=±Rx=\pm Rx=±R separately.

Watch out

  • Divide every term, constants included. (23)n\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)^n(32​)n shrinks to 000.
  • Check where the sum starts. From n=0n=0n=0 the first term is 111, and the exponent in sNs_NsN​ is N+1N+1N+1.
  • an→0a_n\to0an​→0 alone doesn't make a series converge: 1n→0\dfrac{1}{n}\to0n1​→0, but ∑1n\sum\dfrac{1}{n}∑n1​ diverges.

Day 10 & 11 · 26 & 27 Oct · Quiz 05

Newton's method and Taylor series

  • Newton's method: xn+1=xn−f(xn)f′(xn)x_{n+1}=x_n-\frac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}xn+1​=xn​−f′(xn​)f(xn​)​ Each xnx_nxn​ is an approximation of the root, not the root.
  • When it's guaranteed on [a,b][a,b][a,b]: f(a)f(a)f(a) and f(b)f(b)f(b) have opposite signs, and f′f'f′ and f′′f''f′′ don't change sign. Start at the endpoint where f(x1) f′′(x1)>0.f(x_1)\,f''(x_1)>0.f(x1​)f′′(x1​)>0.
  • Linear approximation: f(x)≈f(a)+f′(a)(x−a).f(x)\approx f(a)+f'(a)(x-a).f(x)≈f(a)+f′(a)(x−a). Concave down means the estimate is too big; concave up, too small.
  • Taylor coefficients: ck=f(k)(a)k!c_k=\frac{f^{(k)}(a)}{k!}ck​=k!f(k)(a)​ Simplify first: cos⁡2x−sin⁡2x=cos⁡2x\cos^2x-\sin^2x=\cos 2xcos2x−sin2x=cos2x and sin⁡xcos⁡x=12sin⁡2x.\sin x\cos x=\frac{1}{2}\sin 2x.sinxcosx=21​sin2x.
  • Taylor polynomial: pn(x)=∑k=0nck(x−a)kp_n(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}c_k(x-a)^kpn​(x)=k=0∑n​ck​(x−a)k With a=0a=0a=0 it's called a Maclaurin polynomial.

Watch out

  • Watch the signs in x−ff′x-\dfrac{f}{f'}x−f′f​ when fff is negative, and the decimals: 110=0.1\frac{1}{10}=0.1101​=0.1.
  • Divide by k!k!k!: c2=f′′(a)2c_2=\dfrac{f''(a)}{2}c2​=2f′′(a)​ and c3=f′′′(a)6.c_3=\dfrac{f'''(a)}{6}.c3​=6f′′′(a)​.

Day 12 · 29 Oct · Not on the midterm

Introduction to differential equation

An introduction only. It isn't on the midterm, and differential equations are covered in full in a later semester.

  • What it is: an equation linking an unknown function y(x)y(x)y(x) with its derivatives, like y′=2yy'=2yy′=2y. Solving it means finding every function that makes it true. The order is the highest derivative: y′=2yy'=2yy′=2y is first order, and y′′+y=0y''+y=0y′′+y=0 is second order.
  • Checking a solution: differentiate the given yyy and substitute it into both sides. For y=Ce2xy=Ce^{2x}y=Ce2x, y′=2Ce2x=2yy'=2Ce^{2x}=2yy′=2Ce2x=2y, so it solves y′=2yy'=2yy′=2y for every CCC.
  • Ambiguity of the solution: the equation alone doesn't fix one function, because constants disappear when you differentiate. y′=2xy'=2xy′=2x is solved by y=x2+Cy=x^2+Cy=x2+C for any CCC. The general solution has as many free constants as the order.
  • Initial conditions: a value such as y(0)=3y(0)=3y(0)=3 picks one curve from the family. Solve first and keep CCC, then substitute the condition, solve for CCC and write the function. You need one condition per constant, usually y(0)y(0)y(0) and y′(0)y'(0)y′(0) for second order.
  • y′=f(x)y'=f(x)y′=f(x): integrate, y=∫f(x) dx+C.y=\int f(x)\,dx+C.y=∫f(x)dx+C. With f′(x)=1xf'(x)=\dfrac{1}{x}f′(x)=x1​ and f(1)=0f(1)=0f(1)=0, f(x)=ln⁡xf(x)=\ln xf(x)=lnx. With f′(x)=exf'(x)=e^xf′(x)=ex and f(0)=ef(0)=ef(0)=e, f(x)=ex+e−1f(x)=e^x+e-1f(x)=ex+e−1.
  • y′=λyy'=\lambda yy′=λy: since (eλx)′=λeλx,(e^{\lambda x})'=\lambda e^{\lambda x},(eλx)′=λeλx, the general solution is y=Ceλxy=Ce^{\lambda x}y=Ceλx, and C=y(0)C=y(0)C=y(0). Here CCC multiplies instead of being added. It grows for λ>0\lambda>0λ>0 and decays for λ<0\lambda<0λ<0.
  • Why only CeλxCe^{\lambda x}Ceλx: dividing by yyy gives (ln⁡∣y∣)′=λ,(\ln|y|)'=\lambda,(ln∣y∣)′=λ, so ln⁡∣y∣=λx+c\ln|y|=\lambda x+cln∣y∣=λx+c and y=±eceλx.y=\pm e^{c}e^{\lambda x}.y=±eceλx. Together with y=0y=0y=0, that is CeλxCe^{\lambda x}Ceλx for any real CCC.
  • Second order, y′′+ay′+by=0y''+ay'+by=0y′′+ay′+by=0: try y=eλxy=e^{\lambda x}y=eλx. Then (λ2+aλ+b)eλx=0,(\lambda^2+a\lambda+b)e^{\lambda x}=0,(λ2+aλ+b)eλx=0, and since eλx≠0,e^{\lambda x}\ne0,eλx=0, the characteristic equation λ2+aλ+b=0\lambda^2+a\lambda+b=0λ2+aλ+b=0 must hold. If y1y_1y1​ and y2y_2y2​ are solutions, so is C1y1+C2y2C_1y_1+C_2y_2C1​y1​+C2​y2​.
  • Three cases, by the sign of Δ=a2−4b\Delta=a^2-4bΔ=a2−4b, writing complex roots as λ=α±βi\lambda=\alpha\pm\beta iλ=α±βi: Δ>0: y=C1eλ1x+C2eλ2xΔ=0: y=(C1+C2x)eλxΔ<0: y=eαx(C1cos⁡βx+C2sin⁡βx)\begin{aligned}\Delta>0&:\ y=C_1e^{\lambda_1x}+C_2e^{\lambda_2x}\\ \Delta=0&:\ y=(C_1+C_2x)e^{\lambda x}\\ \Delta<0&:\ y=e^{\alpha x}(C_1\cos\beta x+C_2\sin\beta x)\end{aligned}Δ>0Δ=0Δ<0​: y=C1​eλ1​x+C2​eλ2​x: y=(C1​+C2​x)eλx: y=eαx(C1​cosβx+C2​sinβx)​ For Δ=0\Delta=0Δ=0, xeλxxe^{\lambda x}xeλx is a second solution because 2λ+a=02\lambda+a=02λ+a=0. For Δ<0\Delta<0Δ<0, Euler's formula eiθ=cos⁡θ+isin⁡θe^{i\theta}=\cos\theta+i\sin\thetaeiθ=cosθ+isinθ turns the complex exponentials into cos⁡\coscos and sin⁡\sinsin.

Watch out

  • Solve the equation first, then use the condition, and end with the function itself, not just "C=…C=\dotsC=…".
  • The given value goes on the right: f(0)=ef(0)=ef(0)=e means 1+C=e1+C=e1+C=e, so C=e−1C=e-1C=e−1, not −1-1−1.
  • CCC is the starting value only when the condition is at x=0x=0x=0. For y=Ce−2xy=Ce^{-2x}y=Ce−2x with y(1)=5y(1)=5y(1)=5, Ce−2=5Ce^{-2}=5Ce−2=5 gives C=5e2C=5e^{2}C=5e2, not e−2e^{-2}e−2.
  • A condition on y′y'y′ goes into the formula for y′y'y′, so differentiate the general solution first.
  • With a repeated root, C1eλx+C2eλxC_1e^{\lambda x}+C_2e^{\lambda x}C1​eλx+C2​eλx is really one constant. The second solution is xeλxxe^{\lambda x}xeλx.

Exam-day habits

  • Rewrite every "·" as × before plugging in, and look for a zero factor.
  • Solve equations completely: x2=1x^2=1x2=1 gives ±1\pm1±1, and a cubic can hide a double root.
  • After differentiating, check every term: two terms for a product, a y′y'y′ on every yyy-term, the inner derivative for a chain.
  • Keep answers exact. Without a calculator, 22\frac{\sqrt2}{2}22​​, ln⁡78\ln\frac{7}{8}ln87​ and 2+e2+e2+e are finished answers.
